issues.item: Triggers: Animal Phobia: Talks or photos about snakes
issues.explanation: The trigger set is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. Snakes, dogs, and fire/flames imply unrelated fear contexts and do not form a coherent trigger pattern for the same trauma.

Threat items suggesting generalized hypervigilance to sudden movements and staying alert at night fit assault/combat-type danger better than a child's medical illness, and are not plausibly linked to the selected illness-unrelated triggers.

The appraisal 'nothing has been done about it' implies unresolved wrongdoing or preventable harm, which is difficult to align with the rest of the profile centered on a child's illness rather than interpersonal threat or institutional neglect.

Fire/flames and dogs do not have an obvious clinical link to this trauma, and with no illness-related cues present the trigger profile looks more like a different trauma context. This is more than merely unusual because the trigger node lacks any plausible anchor to the stated event.

Threat items implying immediate danger from other people's sudden movements and needing to stay alert at night suggest a physical assault/combat-style threat context. For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, these threat beliefs are difficult to connect to the trauma and are not supported by the memory or trigger content.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'nothing has been done about it' fits traumas involving perpetration, negligence, or unresolved accountability. In the context of a child's life-threatening illness, this wording is hard to justify unless there were explicit medical errors or blame-related details, which are absent elsewhere in the profile, making this item clinically incoherent with the rest of the formulation.

The trigger set is poorly matched to the trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness. Pregnancy/birth reminders could plausibly connect to a child-focused medical trauma, but 'dogs' and 'alcohol smell' lack an evident clinical link unless the illness involved a dog attack or alcohol-related context, which is not reflected anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items suggest an interpersonal/physical attack context ('sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard', needing to stay alert at night for danger) rather than a child illness trauma. For a parent's trauma involving a child's illness, threat is more typically about recurrence, medical crises, or inability to protect the child, not immediate guarding against others' movements.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it' implies a perpetrator, negligence, or unresolved external wrongdoing. That appraisal can occur after medical trauma, but in this profile there are no memory, trigger, or threat items indicating medical error, institutional betrayal, or blame context, so it sits awkwardly with the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: Pregnancy/birth/babies reminders are hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma of a child's life-threatening illness. For this trauma type, child-health, hospital, medical, or illness-related cues would be expected; pregnancy/childbirth cues imply a different trauma context unless there is additional undisclosed perinatal trauma.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
issues.explanation: The appraisal that 'nothing has been done about it' fits neglect, betrayal, or preventable harm more than a child's serious illness. In the context of a life-threatening illness, the unfairness element is plausible, but the added idea that nothing has been done is clinically discordant unless there was clear medical negligence, which is not otherwise reflected in the profile.

Alcohol smell is not well aligned with the stated trauma type of a child's life-threatening illness, while the other trigger items are strongly medical/hospital-based. Without any corroborating trauma content suggesting alcohol was central to the child's illness experience, this item looks clinically out of place within the trigger set.

issues.item: Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it
issues.explanation: 'Cannot trust safety' suggests a pervasive current danger appraisal more typical of interpersonal violence, combat, or repeated external threat. For a trauma centered on a child's life-threatening illness, this can occur, but here it is not well supported by the rest of the profile, which is focused on medical reminders and reliving rather than generalized danger.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: Sleep vigilance because one 'need[s] to stay alert' implies ongoing monitoring for imminent threat. In the context of a child's past life-threatening illness, this is difficult to reconcile unless there is corresponding material about night-time monitoring, medical deterioration, or responsibility for detecting danger, which is absent from the selected items.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: The hospital/medical trigger pattern fits a child's life-threatening illness, but a burnt-smell danger cue is hard to reconcile with that trauma context unless there is specific unreported trauma-related meaning. As selected, it stands out as clinically implausible relative to the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
issues.explanation: The olfactory memory item implies the original trauma involved a distinctive smell that is re-experienced. In this profile, the only corroborating smell tied to the trauma context should be hospital/antiseptic cues; pairing it with a burnt-smell trigger creates an incoherent sensory trauma context for a child's medical illness.

vignette:
Rajan had spent most of his adult life in situations where other people relied on his steadiness, first as a bomb disposal technician and later, in retirement, as the man family and neighbours still described as calm in a crisis. That long history of control made the period after his son's illness feel even more humiliating to him. At 58, married and living with his wife in the same South Asian community where their children had grown up, Rajan found himself undone by something he could not dismantle, predict, or secure: his child lying critically ill in hospital.

It began when his son was admitted with a life-threatening illness and Rajan sat through long hours in corridors that smelled sharply of antiseptic. The smell stayed with him even after he left the ward, and now it could seize him instantly in a clinic, a pharmacy aisle, or sometimes just at the entrance to a hospital. He would catch that clean, chemical scent and feel as if he had been dropped back into those first days, waiting for news that might change with each doctor's appearance. The sight of needles, drips, and other medical equipment was just as potent. A nurse adjusting an IV line or a tray of syringes could make him go rigid before he had time to look away, his chest tightening and his body reacting with a force that startled him. He had also found himself increasingly uneasy around children, especially in places where they were running, laughing, or being carried by parents. What should have felt ordinary now had an edge of dread, because children were no longer just children to him; they were reminders of how quickly the safety of family life could be shattered.

At the time of the illness, Rajan had tried to stay useful. He had sat by the bed, watched the monitors, and listened to the staff explain procedures he did not fully understand. But even then he knew there were moments he could not control. His son could deteriorate, alarms could sound, and Rajan could do nothing to prevent it. Since then he had come to believe, with a bleak certainty that embarrassed him, that he was a weak person because his reactions were so strong. He had spent years being the one others turned to, yet now his own mind betrayed him with sudden fear, horror, anger, and guilt. Sometimes he was struck by the conviction that his reactions meant he was going crazy. He would be sitting at home, or standing in line somewhere, and a smell or a glimpse of medical tubing could instantly bring back the full memory without warning. When that happened, the memory did not arrive like an ordinary recollection. It came back as a complete sensory reliving, vivid and enveloping, with the hospital corridor, the harsh light, the antiseptic smell, and the sight of equipment all seeming present at once. He often described the memories as pictures first, as if he were seeing the scene in still frames before it swallowed him whole.

These episodes left him unsettled and watchful. At night he had difficulty falling asleep because he felt he needed to stay alert, as though lowering his guard might allow something terrible to happen again. Even after the immediate medical crisis had passed, he could not shake the sense that bad things could come without warning and that he could not stop them. That helplessness sat heavily with him. It made him scan for danger in places where he used to feel at ease and made ordinary family outings more complicated. His wife noticed that he was more hesitant about going to hospitals for his own appointments, and when family gatherings included young children, he often positioned himself at the edge of the room, not wanting to draw attention to the fact that he was trying to manage himself. He disliked what this did to him. The man who once worked with explosives and trusted procedure now felt exposed by a smell, a needle, or a child's sudden laughter.

By the time he sought help, the pattern had become hard to ignore. He was not looking for someone to tell him that the illness never happened; he knew exactly what had happened. What he wanted was some way to understand why his body and mind still reacted as if the danger were immediate, and whether he could sleep without feeling he had to keep watch. More than anything, Rajan feared that these reactions were proof that he was losing his mind, and he hoped that treatment might help him feel like himself again - steady, capable, and no longer at the mercy of memories that arrived unbidden and felt all too real.
